name: Priya Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a small independent in the market town, four of us, and we've started taking hybrids that the main dealer charges a fortune for. I'm the one who reads the fault codes and the wiring diagrams, usually with an AI app open on my phone explaining what the diagram means. My spanner work is still slow, honestly, the older guys can do a timing belt in half my time. What I love is the puzzle, the intermittent faults nobody else wants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside the garage, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Dev, who drives deliveries for a parcel firm. We rent a flat with a damp bedroom we don't use, and I've got about two weeks of money in the bank. The pay's bottom of the range, because I came into the trade late after retail. There's nowhere else round here doing hybrids, so this is pretty much the only door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was silly, but the tools are still handy. I'd keep posting the odd thing about using the app for wiring diagrams, because it genuinely helps. Online I'd say mechanics shouldn't be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau is fine for my job but not for my bank account. Two weeks of savings is two weeks, AI or no AI. And Dev's routes keep getting longer with the same pay, so we're squeezed either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and push the boss to let me take the high-voltage course, because that's where the work is going regardless. I'd stop the streaming subscriptions and look for weekend shifts fixing e-bikes at the bike shop. Anything to build a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but the money isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the boss think of you using AI on the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He laughed at first, called it my magic phone. Then I found a corroded earth on a hybrid that he'd been chasing for two days, using the app to read the diagram. He stopped laughing after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the e-bike shifts came through, what would that money go to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing the damp room first, honestly, a dehumidifier and paint. Then a month of rent in the bank. I've never had a month of rent in the bank.

say: The hype was **silly**, but the tools are still handy for **wiring diagrams**.
I'd tell other mechanics online **not to be scared** of AI.
think: A plateau is fine for my job but not for my **bank account**.
Dev's delivery routes keep **getting longer** for the same pay, so we're squeezed anyway.
do: Push the boss to fund the **high-voltage course** for hybrids and electric cars.
Cancel **streaming subscriptions** to save a little each month.
Look for **weekend shifts** fixing e-bikes at the bike shop.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a safe-feeling job but money that isn't.
S0.quote: I've never had a month of rent in the bank.
fieldNote: Priya is already an **everyday AI user** at work, and proved its value to a sceptical boss.
Her worry in a plateau is purely **money and housing**, not technology.
Her partner's **delivery job** adds a second, separate squeeze.

steps.text: Ask the boss to fund the high-voltage vehicle course
Pick up weekend e-bike repair shifts at the bike shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where mechanics who use the tools pull ahead, and I'd want everyone to get training, not just the young ones. The garage owners should be made to share the gains with the people doing the work. I'd say both, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps me for a while. The thinking side, the codes and diagrams and quotes, gets easier, and I'm already good at that bit. The risk is the boss decides one mechanic with AI does the work of two, and I'm still the slowest with a spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every tool the garage gets, and offer to set up the booking and parts software so I'm the one who runs it. I'd do the high-voltage course this year. I'd keep the e-bike work going on Saturdays so I've got a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit nervous underneath. For the first time, being good with tech counts for something in a garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one mechanic with AI does the work of two. Who would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Gav, the other junior, who's faster than me with tools but can't read a fault code to save his life. Or me, if the boss thinks diagnosis is now free. I'd want us both kept, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dev in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's the one I worry about. The parcel firm already plans his route with software, and they've talked about vans that drive themselves on the motorway bits. He'd need to move before I would.

say: Mechanics who use the tools will **pull ahead**, and everyone should get training.
Owners should be made to **share the gains** with workers.
think: Easier codes and quotes help me, since **diagnosis** is my strongest part.
The risk is one mechanic with AI replacing two, and I'm **slowest with a spanner**.
do: Learn **every new tool** and offer to run the booking and parts software.
Keep **Saturday e-bike work** as a second skill.
S1.quote: For the first time, being good with tech counts for something in a garage.
fieldNote: Priya sees Steady Disruption as a **personal opening**, since she already owns the thinking side.
She'd still defend **Gav, the other junior**, which fits her progressive values.
Her deeper worry shifts to **Dev's delivery job** and its route software.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up and run the garage's booking and parts software
Complete the high-voltage vehicle course this year
Keep fixing e-bikes at the bike shop on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying we need a plan for everyone, now, not later. Things like income support and free retraining paid for by the companies that own the AI. I'd be in every group chat making noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my edge disappears in 2028. If AI can diagnose better than anyone, my one strength is the free bit. Then I'm a slow pair of hands until 2031, when robots do the hands bit too. I'm twenty-seven with two weeks of savings, so that's not a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get in early with whatever companies install and repair the robots, because someone has to fix them at first. I'd look at the local college for a robotics maintenance course and apply for any grant going. I'd cut back hard and save everything from the e-bike work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but buzzing a bit too, which is weird. Like standing at the top of a steep hill on a bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to fix the robots. How long would that last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe a few years, until robots fix robots. But a few years is a few years, and I'd rather be in the robot repair queue than the one for the jobcentre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, since Dev's got the van. Then the holiday we've been saving for, which is only three hundred quid anyway. We'd also talk about moving to Dev's mum's for a year to save rent, which neither of us wants.

say: We need a plan **now**, with **income support** and free retraining paid by AI firms.
I'd be making noise in **every group chat**.
think: My **diagnosis edge** becomes worthless in 2028, leaving me a slow pair of hands.
Robots take the hands-on work by **2031**, and I have little runway.
do: Apply to firms that **install and repair robots**, getting in early.
Look for a **robotics maintenance course** at the local college with a grant.
Cut back and **save all** the e-bike money.
feel: **Frightened** but oddly **buzzing**, like the top of a steep hill.
S2.quote: A few years is a few years, and I'd rather be in the robot repair queue than the one for the jobcentre.
fieldNote: Priya sees the 2028 date as killing her **main advantage**, diagnosis, before robots arrive.
Her answer is to **chase the new work** fixing robots, while admitting it may not last.
She mixes **fear and excitement**, typical of her adaptive temperament.

steps.text: Apply to firms installing and repairing robots
Enrol in a robotics maintenance course at the college with a grant
Sell the car and save all the e-bike money
Move into Dev's mum's for a year to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but calmer: use the five years. Companies should fund training and the government should make sure it happens. I'd also be telling every mechanic I know to get on the electric courses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get properly qualified in something new. By 2031 the diagnosis side is gone, but I'd have the high-voltage ticket and maybe robotics. Then by 2034 I'd want to be the person who looks after the machines, not the person they replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the high-voltage course. Years two and three, a part-time robotics or electrical course at the college while I keep working. I'd start saving properly, fifty a week if the e-bike money holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but focused. Like having a deadline you can actually meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, always. If the garage has a quiet winter or Dev loses his routes, the course goes first. Two weeks of savings can't carry a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to Gav about doing it with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd drag him along. He's brilliant with his hands and terrified of screens. If robots need someone who knows engines and someone who knows software, we'd be a good pair.

say: Use the **five years**, with companies funding training and government making sure.
Every mechanic should get on **electric courses** now.
think: Five years is enough to get **properly qualified** in something new.
By **2034** I want to look after the machines, not be replaced by them.
do: Take the **high-voltage course** in year one.
Study **robotics or electrical** part-time in years two and three.
Save **fifty pounds a week** if the e-bike work holds.
feel: **Nervous but focused**, like a deadline I can meet.
S3.quote: Two weeks of savings can't carry a plan.
fieldNote: Five years gives Priya a **clear sequence** of courses, but money still threatens it.
She stays anxious because one **quiet winter** or Dev losing routes would sink the plan.
She imagines teaming with **Gav**, pairing hands-on and software skills.

steps.text: Take the high-voltage course in the first year
Study robotics part-time at the college in years two and three
Save fifty pounds a week from e-bike repairs
Keep weekend e-bike shifts going to fund courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and the trade should use it to train everyone, apprentices and old hands alike. I'd want a public plan, not just firms doing what suits them. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I might end up running a little workshop myself. Electric, hybrids, maybe the early robots. The money's the problem, because you can't plan a business on two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the high-voltage course, then a few years building up skills and savings properly. I'd look into a co-op workshop with a couple of other mechanics, sharing the tools and the risk. I'd keep using AI for everything on the admin side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, honestly, but still nervous about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op? Why that rather than your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because none of us has the money alone, and I'd rather share the risk than borrow it. I like the idea of the people doing the work owning the place. That's just how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you might move to Dev's mum's. Here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, in this one we'd stay put and try to save for a deposit. Ten years is enough to get the damp room fixed and the bank account above zero.

say: Ten years is **a real chance** to train apprentices and old hands alike.
We need a **public plan**, not firms doing what suits them.
think: With ten years I might run **a little workshop** for electric cars and early robots.
You can't plan a business on **two weeks of savings**.
do: Take the **high-voltage course**, then build skills and savings for a few years.
Explore a **co-op workshop** with other mechanics to share tools and risk.
Use **AI for admin** across quotes, bookings and parts.
S4.quote: I'd rather share the risk than borrow it. I like the idea of the people doing the work owning the place.
fieldNote: A decade makes Priya think like a **founder**, not an employee.
Her progressive values shape the plan into a **co-op**, not a solo business.
Thin savings keep her **anxious** even in the slowest scenario.

steps.text: Complete the high-voltage course in the first year
Explore a co-op workshop with two other mechanics
Run quotes, bookings and parts lists through AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My one strength goes first and the robots come for the rest before I've caught my breath. What would help is paid retraining that doesn't need savings, and some kind of income floor while you're learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being a woman in a garage, which is fine, but it matters. I fought to get in this trade late, and the idea of the trade vanishing just as I've earned my place stings.

headlineQuote: I fought to get in this trade late, and the idea of the trade vanishing just as I've earned my place stings.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** junior at a four-person garage that has started taking hybrids.
She came into the trade late from retail and has about **two weeks** of savings.
She uses AI **every day** to read wiring diagrams and fault codes, but is slow with a spanner.
She sees **opportunity** in slower change, but alarm in 2028 when her diagnosis edge vanishes.
Her progressive views show in wanting **shared gains**, public plans and a co-op workshop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, wiping out her diagnosis skill and then hands-on work within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** needing no savings, plus an **income floor** while learning.
